lessons.title: Reverse differentiation and recover a curve
lessons.summary: Find a family of curves from a gradient function and select the one that passes through a stated point.
lessons.objective: Find a family of curves from a gradient function and select the one that passes through a stated point.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
Integration reverses differentiation by finding functions with the specified derivative.

Adding any constant makes a vertical translation whose derivative is unchanged.

A point gives an input and output for the antiderivative.
lessons.method:
What is being reversed?

Check the antiderivative by differentiating back to the integrand.

Why is there an arbitrary constant?

Write the general antiderivative with the arbitrary constant before substituting a condition.

How does a point select one curve?

Substitute both coordinates, solve for the constant and then evaluate the particular function.
mistakes: A derivative alone does not determine the constant value.
Omitting the constant loses all but one of the possible curves.
The gradient at a point is different from the point's y-coordinate.

examples.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
examples.question:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=21 x^{2} - 1\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + 7 x^{3}\)
  2. \(C + 7 x^{3} - 2 x\)
  3. \(C + 7 x^{3} - x\)
  4. \(7 x^{3} - x\)
examples.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(21 x^{2} - 1\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 7 x^{3} - x\).

examples.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
examples.question:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-1 + \frac{9}{2 \sqrt{x}}\). Use \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + 9 \sqrt{x}\)
  2. \(C + 9 \sqrt{x} - 2 x\)
  3. \(C + 9 \sqrt{x} - x\)
  4. \(9 \sqrt{x} - x\)
examples.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(-1 + \frac{9}{2 \sqrt{x}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 9 \sqrt{x} - x\).

examples.title: Recover a particular curve from its gradient
examples.question:
A curve has gradient function \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-5 - \frac{6}{x^{2}}\). Use \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C - 4 x + \frac{6}{x}\)
  2. \(C - 6 x + \frac{6}{x}\)
  3. \(C - 5 x + \frac{6}{x}\)
  4. \(- 5 x + \frac{6}{x}\)
examples.solution:
Find a function whose derivative is the stated gradient. Add the unknown constant.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(-5 - \frac{6}{x^{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 5 x + \frac{6}{x}\).

lessons.title: Indefinite integrals of powers
lessons.summary: Integrate sums of powers, simplifiable quotients and rational powers with the correct restrictions.
lessons.objective: Integrate sums of powers, simplifiable quotients and rational powers with the correct restrictions.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
For \(n\ne-1\), add one to the exponent n and then divide by the new exponent.

Rewrite a root or reciprocal as a rational power. Keep the original domain.

Expanding a short square and dividing each term by the denominator can reveal standard integrands.
lessons.method:
What happens to an exponent when integrating?

Integrate term by term. Add a single arbitrary constant at the end.

How do you integrate roots and negative powers?

Increase the exponent by one, then divide by that new value, provided it is non-zero.

When is it helpful to divide a quotient term by term?

Simplify the integrand. Integrate a reciprocal x term as a natural logarithm on the appropriate domain.
mistakes: Dividing by the old exponent does not reverse the power rule.
For a reciprocal squared, the new exponent is negative one rather than zero.
Do not integrate the numerator and denominator separately.

examples.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
examples.question:
The integrand is \(9 x^{3} - 11 x + 2\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + \frac{9 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{11 x^{2}}{2} + 3 x\)
  2. \(C + \frac{9 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{11 x^{2}}{2} + x\)
  3. \(C + \frac{9 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{11 x^{2}}{2} + 2 x\)
  4. \(\frac{9 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{11 x^{2}}{2} + 2 x\)
examples.solution:
Integrate each power after simplifying.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(9 x^{3} - 11 x + 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{9 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{11 x^{2}}{2} + 2 x\).

examples.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
examples.question:
The integrand is \(10 \sqrt{x} + 7 + \frac{7}{x^{2}}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + \frac{20 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 8 x - \frac{7}{x}\)
  2. \(C + \frac{20 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 6 x - \frac{7}{x}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{20 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 7 x - \frac{7}{x}\)
  4. \(\frac{20 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 7 x - \frac{7}{x}\)
examples.solution:
Integrate each power after simplifying.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(10 \sqrt{x} + 7 + \frac{7}{x^{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{20 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 7 x - \frac{7}{x}\).

examples.title: Integrate powers and use a point to fix the constant
examples.question:
The integrand is \(\frac{\left(12 x + 6\right)^{2}}{x^{2}}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + 145 x + 144 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{36}{x}\)
  2. \(C + 143 x + 144 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{36}{x}\)
  3. \(C + 144 x + 144 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{36}{x}\)
  4. \(144 x + 144 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{36}{x}\)
examples.solution:
Expand and divide each term by \(x^2\) to write the integrand as \(144 + \frac{144}{x} + \frac{36}{x^{2}}\). The \(\frac{1}{x}\) term integrates to a logarithm on the positive domain.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{\left(12 x + 6\right)^{2}}{x^{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 144 x + 144 \ln{\left(x \right)} - \frac{36}{x}\).

lessons.title: Powers of a linear expression
lessons.summary: Integrate positive, negative and fractional powers of a linear bracket using the reverse chain factor.
lessons.objective: Integrate positive, negative and fractional powers of a linear bracket using the reverse chain factor.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
Differentiating a power of a linear bracket multiplies by the derivative of the bracket.

The new power can still be fractional. Work on the interval where the expression is real.

Add one to the exponent and check the result is non-zero.
lessons.method:
Why divide by the inner slope?

Use the ordinary integration power rule on the bracket and divide by the inner slope.

How do you handle a fractional bracket power?

Leave the bracket intact. Use exact values for convenient bracket inputs.

How does a negative bracket power integrate?

Choose an antiderivative on the stated domain and check by differentiating.
mistakes: The inner slope is a constant, but it still affects the factor.
Do not take a root of a negative argument in a real-valued question.
If the old exponent is −1, use a logarithm rather than dividing by zero.

examples.title: Integrate a power of a linear expression
examples.question:
The integrand is \(5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{2}\) on the interval where \(3 x - 5>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + \frac{5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{3}}{9}\)
  2. \(C - x + \frac{5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{3}}{9}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{3}}{9}\)
  4. \(\frac{5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{3}}{9}\)
examples.solution:
Raise the bracket power by one and divide by that new power and by the inner coefficient \(3\).

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{2}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{5 \left(3 x - 5\right)^{3}}{9}\).

examples.title: Integrate a power of a linear expression
examples.question:
The integrand is \(11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\) on the interval where \(4 x + 4>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + \frac{11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{10}\)
  2. \(C - x + \frac{11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{10}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{10}\)
  4. \(\frac{11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{10}\)
examples.solution:
Raise the bracket power by one and divide by that new power and by the inner coefficient \(4\).

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{11 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{10}\).

examples.title: Integrate a power of a linear expression
examples.question:
The integrand is \(\frac{9}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{4}}\) on the interval where \(3 x + 6>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x - \frac{1}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{3}}\)
  2. \(C - x - \frac{1}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{3}}\)
  3. \(C - \frac{1}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{3}}\)
  4. \(- \frac{1}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{3}}\)
examples.solution:
Raise the bracket power by one and divide by that new power and by the inner coefficient \(3\).

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{9}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{4}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - \frac{1}{\left(3 x + 6\right)^{3}}\).

lessons.title: Integration of exponential functions
lessons.summary: Reverse the exponential derivative and evaluate exact exponential bounds.
lessons.objective: Reverse the exponential derivative and evaluate exact exponential bounds.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
An exponential with a linear exponent stays exponential.

Dividing by the negative inner slope creates a negative coefficient.

Use the appropriate antiderivative term by term.
lessons.method:
What stays when an exponential integrates?

Keep the exponent unchanged and divide by its x-coefficient.

What if the exponent's slope is negative?

Evaluate both endpoints using the same correctly signed antiderivative.

How do you integrate an exponential with other terms?

Keep exact exponentials until a decimal answer is requested. Include the arbitrary constant for an indefinite integral.
mistakes: Changing the exponent itself gives a different derivative.
The integral of a positive function over forward limits is positive.
Round once at the end rather than rounding each exponential separately.

examples.title: Integrate an exponential expression and evaluate its net change
examples.question:
Take the integrand \(3 e^{7 x - 9}\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + \frac{3 e^{7 x - 9}}{7}\)
  2. \(C - x + \frac{3 e^{7 x - 9}}{7}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{3 e^{7 x - 9}}{7}\)
  4. \(\frac{3 e^{7 x - 9}}{7}\)
examples.solution:
Keep the exponential and divide by the coefficient \(7\) of x in its exponent.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(3 e^{7 x - 9}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{3 e^{7 x - 9}}{7}\).

examples.title: Integrate an exponential expression and evaluate its net change
examples.question:
Take the integrand \(12 e^{8 - 2 x}\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x - 6 e^{8 - 2 x}\)
  2. \(C - x - 6 e^{8 - 2 x}\)
  3. \(C - 6 e^{8 - 2 x}\)
  4. \(- 6 e^{8 - 2 x}\)
examples.solution:
Keep the exponential and divide by the coefficient \(-2\) of x in its exponent.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(12 e^{8 - 2 x}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 6 e^{8 - 2 x}\).

examples.title: Integrate an exponential expression and evaluate its net change
examples.question:
Take the integrand \(5 x + 2 e^{10 x + 10}\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + \frac{5 x^{2}}{2} + x + \frac{e^{10 x + 10}}{5}\)
  2. \(C + \frac{5 x^{2}}{2} - x + \frac{e^{10 x + 10}}{5}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{5 x^{2}}{2} + \frac{e^{10 x + 10}}{5}\)
  4. \(\frac{5 x^{2}}{2} + \frac{e^{10 x + 10}}{5}\)
examples.solution:
Keep the exponential and divide by the coefficient \(10\) of x in its exponent.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(5 x + 2 e^{10 x + 10}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{5 x^{2}}{2} + \frac{e^{10 x + 10}}{5}\).

lessons.title: Integrals of sine, cosine and secant squared
lessons.summary: Use radian antiderivatives, exact special-angle values and the reverse chain factor.
lessons.objective: Use radian antiderivatives, exact special-angle values and the reverse chain factor.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
The derivative of \(-\cos x\) is \(\sin x\).

Sine differentiates to cosine in radian measure.

Tangent differentiates to secant squared when the angle is measured in radians.
lessons.method:
Which antiderivative gives sine?

Use negative cosine, then divide by the inner slope for a linear angle.

Which antiderivative gives cosine?

Use the same angle inside sine and divide by the inner derivative. Combine with the integral of any constant term.

How does tangent appear when integrating?

Use a tangent antiderivative and choose bounds on one continuous branch.
mistakes: Cosine without the negative sign differentiates to negative sine.
A constant term integrates to a multiple of x.
An interval crossing a point where cosine is zero cannot be evaluated with the ordinary finite-bound formula.

examples.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
examples.question:
The integrand is \(- 9 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 4\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C - 3 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  2. \(C - 5 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  3. \(C - 4 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  4. \(- 4 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
examples.solution:
The antiderivative of sine is negative cosine. Then divide by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(- 9 \cos{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} - 4\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 4 x - \frac{9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\).

examples.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
examples.question:
The integrand is \(11 \cos{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} - 2\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C - x + \frac{11 \sin{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{4}\)
  2. \(C - 3 x + \frac{11 \sin{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{4}\)
  3. \(C - 2 x + \frac{11 \sin{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{4}\)
  4. \(- 2 x + \frac{11 \sin{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{4}\)
examples.solution:
Cosine integrates to sine. Divide the sine coefficient by the inner derivative.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(11 \cos{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)} - 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - 2 x + \frac{11 \sin{\left(4 x + \frac{\pi}{6} \right)}}{4}\).

examples.title: Integrate a trigonometric function in radians
examples.question:
The integrand is \(5 \csc^{2}{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} + 2\). Angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + 3 x - \frac{5 \cot{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  2. \(C + x - \frac{5 \cot{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  3. \(C + 2 x - \frac{5 \cot{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
  4. \(2 x - \frac{5 \cot{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\)
examples.solution:
The derivative of tangent is secant squared. Divide by the factor from the bracket.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(5 \csc^{2}{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)} + 2\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 2 x - \frac{5 \cot{\left(8 x + \frac{5 \pi}{14} \right)}}{8}\).

lessons.title: Reciprocal integrals and natural logarithms
lessons.summary: Recognise the power-rule exception and choose a logarithmic form on a valid interval.
lessons.objective: Recognise the power-rule exception and choose a logarithmic form on a valid interval.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
For \(x>0\), differentiating \(\ln x\) gives \(\frac1x\).

The derivative of the denominator is part of the chain rule for a logarithm.

A reciprocal is not continuous where its denominator is zero.
lessons.method:
Why does one over x need a different rule?

Use a natural logarithm instead of the integration power rule at exponent −1.

What factor goes before the logarithm?

For a linear denominator, divide by its x-coefficient and place its absolute value inside the logarithm.

Why must both limits stay on the same side of a pole?

Check that the full interval lies in one continuous branch. Use the log form on that branch.
mistakes: Adding one to −1 would give a zero denominator in the power rule.
A logarithmic antiderivative of a reciprocal has a factor from the denominator.
Two finite endpoint logarithms alone cannot justify an integral across a pole.

examples.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
examples.question:
The integrand is \(\frac{8}{x}\). Work on \(x>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + 8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)
  2. \(C - x + 8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)
  3. \(8\ln\left|x\right|+C\)
  4. \(8 \ln{\left(x \right)}\)
examples.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{8}{x}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(8\ln\left|x\right|+C\).

examples.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
examples.question:
The integrand is \(\frac{11}{6 x - 2}\). Work on \(6 x - 2>0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + x + \frac{11 \ln{\left(6 x - 2 \right)}}{6}\)
  2. \(C - x + \frac{11 \ln{\left(6 x - 2 \right)}}{6}\)
  3. \(\frac{11}{6}\ln\left|6 x - 2\right|+C\)
  4. \(\frac{11 \ln{\left(6 x - 2 \right)}}{6}\)
examples.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{11}{6 x - 2}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(\frac{11}{6}\ln\left|6 x - 2\right|+C\).

examples.title: Integrate a reciprocal and stay on one side of its pole
examples.question:
The integrand is \(-3 + \frac{9}{2 x - 9}\). Work on \(2 x - 9<0\).

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C - 2 x + \frac{9 \ln{\left(9 - 2 x \right)}}{2}\)
  2. \(C - 4 x + \frac{9 \ln{\left(9 - 2 x \right)}}{2}\)
  3. \(\frac{9}{2}\ln\left|2 x - 9\right|- 3 x+C\)
  4. \(- 3 x + \frac{9 \ln{\left(9 - 2 x \right)}}{2}\)
examples.solution:
The integral power rule excludes exponent −1. Use a logarithm and keep the reciprocal of the linear gradient.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(-3 + \frac{9}{2 x - 9}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(\frac{9}{2}\ln\left|2 x - 9\right|- 3 x+C\).

lessons.title: Further indefinite integration
lessons.summary: Select antiderivative rules across mixed sums and verify the complete expression.
lessons.objective: Select antiderivative rules across mixed sums and verify the complete expression.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
The integral of a sum is the sum of its integrals.

All separate additive constants combine into a single constant.

A linear argument contributes its derivative on differentiation. Reverse this factor when integrating.
lessons.method:
How do you organise a sum of different function types?

Identify an exponential, power or trigonometric rule for each term before simplifying.

How many arbitrary constants are needed?

Write all variable terms first, then add one C and check by differentiating.

When do bracketed terms need an extra factor?

Keep the bracket intact unless expanding makes the integral simpler.
mistakes: One power rule does not serve a sum containing different function types.
A missing constant is incomplete for an indefinite integral.
Expanding a term and applying its chain factor as well counts the factor twice.

examples.title: Select the correct antiderivative for each term
examples.question:
Integrate the expression \(x^{3} + 10 e^{9 x + 7}\). Any angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + \frac{x^{4}}{4} + x + \frac{10 e^{9 x + 7}}{9}\)
  2. \(C + \frac{x^{4}}{4} - x + \frac{10 e^{9 x + 7}}{9}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{10 e^{9 x + 7}}{9}\)
  4. \(\frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{10 e^{9 x + 7}}{9}\)
examples.solution:
Integrate the terms separately, keeping each numerical coefficient with its term.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(x^{3} + 10 e^{9 x + 7}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{10 e^{9 x + 7}}{9}\).

examples.title: Select the correct antiderivative for each term
examples.question:
Integrate the expression \(6 x + 7 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\). Any angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + 3 x^{2} + x - \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\)
  2. \(C + 3 x^{2} - x - \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\)
  3. \(C + 3 x^{2} - \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\)
  4. \(3 x^{2} - \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\)
examples.solution:
Integrate the terms separately, keeping each numerical coefficient with its term.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(6 x + 7 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + 3 x^{2} - \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\).

examples.title: Select the correct antiderivative for each term
examples.question:
Integrate the expression \(x + 4 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{3}\). Any angles are in radians.

Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

  1. \(C + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x + \frac{\left(4 x + 4\right)^{4}}{4}\)
  2. \(C + \frac{x^{2}}{2} - x + \frac{\left(4 x + 4\right)^{4}}{4}\)
  3. \(C + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{\left(4 x + 4\right)^{4}}{4}\)
  4. \(\frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{\left(4 x + 4\right)^{4}}{4}\)
examples.solution:
Integrate the terms separately, keeping each numerical coefficient with its term.

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(x + 4 \left(4 x + 4\right)^{3}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{\left(4 x + 4\right)^{4}}{4}\).

lessons.title: Definite integration and signed bounds
lessons.summary: Calculate the upper antiderivative value minus the lower one and interpret a reversed interval.
lessons.objective: Calculate the upper antiderivative value minus the lower one and interpret a reversed interval.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
The definite integral over a continuous interval is the antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

Exchanging the bounds changes the sign of the integral.

The ordinary evaluation uses an antiderivative on an interval where the integrand is continuous.
lessons.method:
Which endpoint is subtracted?

Write both substitutions explicitly before subtracting. An antiderivative's arbitrary constant cancels.

What happens when limits are reversed?

Follow the displayed order. If you choose to rewrite the bounds, carry the negative sign.

What if the function contains a reciprocal?

Check the original integrand for excluded inputs before applying the endpoint formula.
mistakes: Do not ignore the lower substitution even if the lower bound is zero.
The mathematically upper written limit can be numerically smaller than the lower written limit.
A finite answer from substituting at both ends is insufficient if the interval crosses a pole.

examples.title: Use signed limits in a definite integral
examples.question:
The integrand is \(5 x^{3} - 7 x - 6\) on the interval whose endpoints are \(-1\) and \(1\).

Evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{1}5 x^{3} - 7 x - 6\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
examples.solution:
The variable part of an antiderivative is \(\frac{5 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{7 x^{2}}{2} - 6 x\).

Subtract its value at \(-1\) from its value at \(1\).

Answer: \(-12\).

examples.title: Use signed limits in a definite integral
examples.question:
The integrand is \(9 x^{2} - 6 x - 10\) on the interval whose endpoints are \(4\) and \(-3\).

Evaluate \(\int_{4}^{-3}9 x^{2} - 6 x - 10\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.
examples.solution:
The variable part of an antiderivative is \(3 x^{3} - 3 x^{2} - 10 x\).

Subtract its value at \(4\) from its value at \(-3\).

Answer: \(-182\).

lessons.title: Use a known derivative to evaluate an integral
lessons.summary: Recognise a supplied antiderivative and apply it to an exact definite integral.
lessons.objective: Recognise a supplied antiderivative and apply it to an exact definite integral.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
Differentiating it must recover the integrand on the required interval.

A root derivative produces both a square-root denominator and the derivative of its argument.

Once verified, the proposed function can be used directly for the endpoint calculation.
lessons.method:
What evidence proves a proposed antiderivative?

Apply the outer derivative and inner factor, then check that the result matches every term.

How can a root derivative give a related integral?

Spot the full structure, including the numerator, or verify it by differentiating the proposed expression.

How do you use the recognised function at the endpoints?

Find the indefinite integral up to a constant, then evaluate the particular definite integral with exact values.
mistakes: Matching only the bracket power does not check the whole antiderivative.
A root in the denominator alone is not enough to identify the integral.
The two sets of limits are still x-values after using a known derivative.

examples.title: Use a derivative to recognise an antiderivative
examples.question:
The integrand is \(\left(180 x + 54\right) \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{2}\) on \(x\ge0\).

Find the full indefinite integral of the given integrand.

  1. \(C + x + 6 \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{3}\)
  2. \(C + \left(180 x + 54\right) \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{2}\)
  3. \(C + 6 \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{3}\)
  4. \(6 \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{3}\)
examples.solution:
Differentiate \(6 \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{3}\) to obtain \(\left(180 x + 54\right) \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{2}\). All antiderivatives differ by a constant.

Answer: \(C + 6 \left(5 x^{2} + 3 x + 1\right)^{3}\).

lessons.title: Signed integrals and areas under curves
lessons.summary: Find crossings, distinguish signed integral from area and add regions on opposite sides of the axis.
lessons.objective: Find crossings, distinguish signed integral from area and add regions on opposite sides of the axis.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
On an interval where the curve is above or on the x-axis, its integral is the area beneath it.

The integral counts a region below the axis with a negative sign. Its geometric area is positive.

A crossing divides the region into pieces with different signs.
lessons.method:
When does the definite integral equal an area?

Find the appropriate endpoints and check the sign of the integrand in the interval.

Why can the definite integral be negative?

Negate the signed integral for a region that stays below the axis.

How do you add areas across an axis crossing?

Integrate separately on each side of the crossing, then add the geometric areas.
mistakes: A graph with an x-intercept can still lie entirely above the axis on the requested interval.
State the area as a positive value.
Taking the absolute value after adding signed parts can cancel area.

examples.title: Separate geometric area from a signed integral

lessons.title: Areas between lines and curves
lessons.summary: Find intersections, choose the upper curve on each interval and add exact areas.
lessons.objective: Find intersections, choose the upper curve on each interval and add exact areas.
lessons.before: Work through the examples with exact values and show the mathematical steps.
lessons.ideas:
At an intersection the two graphs have equal y-values.

The strip height is upper y minus lower y.

Ordering can change at each intersection.
lessons.method:
Which points provide the limits?

Equate the expressions and solve every admissible root. Use the intersection x-values as limits.

What is the height of a thin vertical strip?

Use an interior x-value to identify the upper function, then integrate the difference.

How do you add regions if the graphs cross more than twice?

Split at every relevant crossing and integrate upper minus lower on each interval before summing.
mistakes: Intercepts of one of the curves are not necessarily the intersections.
Which curve is upper depends on the interval.
One signed integral over both regions can undercount the area.

examples.title: Find the region enclosed by a line and a curve

examples.solution:
Equate the two equations and solve \(- \left(x + 3\right) \left(x + 6\right)=0\).

examples.title: Find the region enclosed by two curves

examples.title: Find the region enclosed by a line and a curve

The integrand is \(\frac{5}{\left(5 x + 8\right)^{3}}\) on the interval where \(5 x + 8>0\).

  1. Find the indefinite integral. Give the full family of antiderivatives.

    [2]

  2. Evaluate \(\int_{- \frac{6}{5}}^{\frac{2}{5}}\frac{5}{\left(5 x + 8\right)^{3}}\,\mathrm dx\) exactly.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Raise the bracket power by one and divide by that new power and by the inner coefficient \(5\).

Differentiating the variable part gives back \(\frac{5}{\left(5 x + 8\right)^{3}}\). Every constant has derivative zero.

Answer: \(C - \frac{1}{2 \left(5 x + 8\right)^{2}}\).

(b)

The variable part of an antiderivative is \(- \frac{1}{2 \left(5 x + 8\right)^{2}}\).

Subtract its value at \(- \frac{6}{5}\) from its value at \(\frac{2}{5}\).

Answer: \(\frac{3}{25}\).
questions.hint_html: Check which constant appears when differentiating the bracket.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the relevant reverse derivative rule and include an arbitrary constant.
Substitute upper and lower bounds into the same antiderivative and subtract in order.

A curve has equation \(y=\left(5 - x\right) \left(6 x + 12\right)\).

  1. Find the x-values where the curve meets the x-axis.

    [2]

  2. Calculate the total area between the curve and the x-axis for \(-2\le x\le 5\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Set \(\left(5 - x\right) \left(6 x + 12\right)\) equal to zero and use the two linear factors.

Answer: \(-2, 5\).

(b)

Use \(- 2 x^{3} + 9 x^{2} + 60 x\) to evaluate the signed integral separately on each of the following bounds.

From \(-2\) to \(5\), the signed integral is \(343\) and the area is \(343\).

Add the positive region areas.

Answer: \(343\).
questions.hint_html: Find crossings first and inspect the sign on every subinterval.

marking_criteria.description_html: Solve both factors of the equation for the x-intercepts.
Split where the sign changes and add the unsigned areas.
